## Force Is Not Work Until Something Moves {#sec-lay-ch10}

## A Concrete Picture

Hold a heavy suitcase motionless for a minute. Your muscles fatigue, but the
suitcase has not moved and the external mechanical work on it is zero. Carry it
horizontally at constant height and the upward hand force is nearly perpendicular
to horizontal velocity, so that force again does little mechanical work on the
suitcase. Lift it onto a shelf and force aligns with displacement; positive work
by the hand raises the suitcase–Earth gravitational potential energy. During a
slow lift, the hand and gravity do nearly equal and opposite work on the suitcase,
so its kinetic energy changes little. Hand work and net work are different ledgers.

This example feels unfair because biological effort is real in all three cases.
That is exactly the lesson. Mechanical work, metabolic cost, muscle activation,
and perceived effort are different quantities. A large grip force may stabilize
the club with little club-level work. A modest force aligned with fast hand motion
may transfer large power.

![Force, Velocity, and Their Projection Distinguish Large Load From Large Mechanical Power.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_force_power_projection.svg){#fig-lay-force-power width=96% fig-alt="Three panels compare force aligned with velocity, opposed to velocity, and perpendicular to velocity, yielding positive, negative, and zero instantaneous power."}

## How the Mechanism Works

Over a path, translational work is

$$W=\int \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r.$$

Here $\mathbf r$ is the position of the material point where the force acts,
measured in a declared inertial observer frame; $\mathbf v=\dot{\mathbf r}$.
Over time, $W=\int \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v\,dt$. For a rigid body, rotational
power at the chosen reference is $\mathbf M\cdot\boldsymbol\omega$, so its work
channel is $\int\mathbf M\cdot\boldsymbol\omega\,dt$. Only for rotation about a
fixed axis does this reduce directly to $\int M_{\rm axis}\,d\theta$.
In general three-dimensional motion, Euler-angle rates are not the components
of angular velocity. Generalized moments must be transformed to be power
conjugate to those rates before taking their dot product.

Impulse instead integrates force over time, $\mathbf J=\int\mathbf F\,dt$.
For a fixed collection of bodies, the **net external** impulse equals the change
in total linear momentum in that inertial frame. A single force contributes to
that balance; other forces may cancel it. These answer different questions.

A force can have large impulse and small work when it acts mostly perpendicular
to motion. It can have small impulse and meaningful work if it aligns with rapid
motion over a short interval. Reporting magnitude, impulse, power, and work
together exposes the difference.

### Hand-Path Force Needs a Declared Path

Some golf analyses project net hand force along the hand path and integrate over
path length. This can be a useful transfer observable. But a large value does not
prove large biological effort. A chosen model may assign much of the instantaneous force to its
drift/constraint part and an opposing contribution to its input part. This is a
decomposition at the same achieved state, not a finding that muscle activity was
unnecessary. Removing an input changes later states and reactions; its causal
effect requires a new trajectory under a declared intervention or controller.

The pinned hand-path study evaluates this estimand in a planar double pendulum,
a one-arm three-link point-mass model, and a two-arm floating-club closed loop. In two
forward cases, drift supplies slightly more than 100% of signed hand-path force
work because the contemporaneous control contribution is opposing. A percentage
above 100 does not violate conservation; positive and negative contributions
cancel to the total. In a prescribed two-arm kinematic sweep, rather than a
forward rollout, drift and control nearly cancel,
making fraction language unstable.

### What the Coriolis-Impulse Search Actually Optimized

A separate archived pendulum example asks a deliberately narrow question: among 135 frozen
torque programs, which one produces the greatest *absolute* along-hand-path
impulse from the coordinate-defined Coriolis cross term before qualified
impact? Absolute impulse counts both signs, so a force that reverses direction
does not disappear through cancellation. Signed impulse is published beside it
to retain sign relative to the changing path tangent. This scalar projected
impulse is not the vector impulse that appears in the momentum balance. The
registered search uses shoulder-absolute and wrist-relative coordinates; its
Coriolis label denotes their cross-speed equation terms. It is not an additional
force acting on a free-body diagram.

The grid combines three proximal torques (60, 80, 100 N m), three restraint
magnitudes (0, 5, 10 N m), and fifteen onset times from 0 to 0.350 s. After onset,
the wrist drive is 15 N m. Ninety-one programs reach the registered event: the
first upward crossing of the club angle through downward vertical, with arm
angle no greater than 2 radians. The other 44 are excluded. This is a geometric
pre-impact score interpolated from sampled history, not a simulated ball collision. The maximum absolute
Coriolis impulse is 13.817 N s with a 100 N m proximal drive, 10 N m of early
wrist restraint, and wrist-drive onset at 0.100 s. That program reaches
46.780 m/s. The highest-speed program also uses 100 N m proximally, but 5 N m of early restraint and
a 0.125 s onset; it reaches 46.913 m/s with 13.701 N s of absolute Coriolis
impulse. The optima are close, but they are not the same program. Maximizing a
named force component is therefore not identical to maximizing clubhead speed,
even inside this small deterministic model. These are discrete grid maxima,
not continuous optimal-control solutions or human swing prescriptions.

The signed values deepen the lesson. The maximum-absolute-impulse program has a
signed Coriolis impulse of -6.825 N s and Coriolis generalized work of
-100.69 J. A large absolute impulse can coexist with negative net work because
the source reverses and because force, velocity, and generalized-coordinate
signs matter. Squared-speed work is -33.73 J, gravity work is +25.56 J, and
applied-drive work is +358.20 J in the same impact-truncated interval. These
figures are an equation-term ledger, not a claim that a Coriolis agent supplied
or removed a measured amount of biological energy. Nor does their sum, by
itself, equal the change in total kinetic energy: the configuration dependence
of the mass matrix matters.

For example, in a smooth ideal model with time-independent constraints, let $q$ be the generalized coordinates,
$M(q)$ the mass matrix, $U(q)$ the potential, and $\tau$ the applied generalized
forces. Define kinetic energy
$K=\tfrac12\dot q^TM(q)\dot q$ and write
$M\ddot q+h+\nabla U=\tau$, with $h$ the full velocity bias and dots denoting time derivatives. The kinetic-energy
rate contains $\tfrac12\dot q^T\dot M\dot q$ as well as
$\dot q^TM\ddot q$. For the usual consistent rigid-body equations,
$\dot q^Th=\tfrac12\dot q^T\dot M\dot q$; these terms cancel to give
$d(K+U)/dt=\tau^T\dot q$. Coriolis and squared-speed terms redistribute the
coordinate acceleration balance without becoming extra energy sources. Include
dissipation, moving constraints and explicit time dependence when they are
present.

### The Hand-Path Arrow Does Not Carry the Whole Wrench

The modeled wrist point moves with the arm coordinate but not independently
with the relative wrist coordinate. Its task Jacobian is therefore
rank-deficient for mapping a two-coordinate generalized drive into one
force-only hand-path vector. The software computes the minimum-norm force that
can be represented at the wrist and keeps the leftover generalized couple as a
residual. It never hides that remainder inside the displayed hand force.
For component $k$, use generalized drive $Q_k$, point Jacobian
$J_H=\partial x_H/\partial q$, mapped force $F_{H,k}$, residual $r_k$,
and point velocity $v_H=J_H\dot q$. Then
$Q_k=J_H^TF_{H,k}+r_k$. Consequently,
$Q_k^T\dot q=F_{H,k}^Tv_H+r_k^T\dot q$. The generalized work totals above
include the residual-power channel; they are not just force work along the hand
path. A least-squares force equivalent is not automatically a measured contact
force.

The archived maximum residual norm is 54.44 N m for the impulse-selected
program and 52.81 N m for the speed-selected program. Each maximum is taken
over time **and all attributed components**, not solely the Coriolis component
or the net physical wrist moment. This is a structural mapping diagnostic, not
a measured joint load or a small numerical rounding error. It tells the reader
that an along-path force plot answers a useful but incomplete question. A
complete grip description needs a wrench, or an endpoint-and-couple mapping
with enough independent coordinates and measurements.

At the top of the simulated swing, hand speed begins at zero, so no path tangent
exists. The integration marks that interval undefined and uses only adjacent
samples with a defined direction (the archived speed threshold is
$10^{-12}$ m/s). Generalized power remains defined at zero speed and its work
is integrated over the full recorded interval. More than 99.6% of the impact-truncated time
is valid in the highlighted runs. Reporting that fraction prevents an arbitrary
initial direction from contaminating the impulse. It does not bound the
missing impulse: even a short excluded interval can matter if its force is
large. Report the masking threshold and convergence when interpreting a small
difference between programs.

### Fractions Become Dangerous Near Cancellation

If drift contributes $+10$ J and control contributes $-9$ J, total signed work
is $+1$ J. Calling drift “1,000% of total” is arithmetically correct and
scientifically awkward. If total crosses zero, the fraction is undefined.

Better reports show signed contributions, absolute magnitudes, a cancellation
index, and intervals separately. Ratios are reserved for denominators safely
away from zero. This is not statistical fussiness; it prevents a small residual
from turning two large opposing mechanisms into a sensational percentage.

### Power Reveals Timing Hidden by Work

Two strategies can deliver the same integrated work with different power
histories. One may load the shaft early and receive energy back late. Another may
deliver direct power near impact. Their club energies at one instant can match
while internal loads and robustness differ.

Plotting cumulative work beside instantaneous power is useful. The power curve
shows when exchange occurs; the cumulative curve shows what remains after
positive and negative intervals cancel. A phase-integrated table connects both
to transition, early downswing, delivery, and impact.

### Joint Power Is Not Muscle Power

A measured or inferred net joint power is a mechanical constraint on a model;
it is not a muscle-energy meter. Tendon storage, biarticular transfer and
opposing muscle forces can produce different biological allocations with the
same net result. The segment-work section below specifies the required
relative angular velocity and explains what inverse dynamics identifies.

This distinction is central to the arm-versus-wrist proposal. A net club wrench
can match while direct wrist moments, two-hand force couples, internal squeeze,
and proximal joint loads vary. Club-level work is an outcome constraint, not a
biological allocation measurement.

**Model Result:** The hand-path attribution separates pointwise drift and control
contributions, then reports impulse, power, work, force vectors, joint effects,
and cancellation rather than one percentage. Recomputing the selections from
the archived 135 outcome records reproduces the stated grid winners and counts.
That check does not independently reproduce their ODE trajectories or quadrature.

**Human Evidence:** Nesbit and Serrano used kinematically driven body/club models
to examine four selected amateur golfers; the outputs are model-based work
estimates, not direct muscle-energy measurements [@nesbit2005work]. MacKenzie
and colleagues analyzed 76 right-handed golfers with handicaps below 15 using
the same driver, inverse dynamics and between-golfer regressions. Their strong
force/work associations do not measure the effect of instructing a golfer to
pull harder [@mackenzie2020energy]. Model boundaries, differentiation, inertial
parameters and shaft treatment affect interpretation. Contact measurements and
muscle-informed models can narrow the ambiguity without eliminating it.

**Practical Interpretation:** Force tells how strongly the system interacts;
work tells how that force aligns with motion over distance; power tells how fast
the exchange happens; effort belongs to a separate biological account.

### From Force History to Mechanical Consequence

Start with a force vector through time. Its integral is that force’s impulse;
only the sum of external impulses fixes the system’s momentum change. Pair each force sample with contact-point velocity and take the dot
product to obtain power. Integrate power for work. Pair a moment with angular
velocity for rotational power. These operations answer related but distinct
questions; none can be safely inferred from the appearance of the force curve.

A high force applied while a point barely moves may create little work. A lower
force acting through a long displacement can do more. A force perpendicular to
velocity can bend a trajectory without changing kinetic energy at that instant.
In a golf swing, all three patterns occur while the club follows a curved,
rotating path.

### The Hand Interface Has Two Power Channels

Choose a club reference point. Translational power is net force dotted with
reference-point velocity. Rotational power is net moment dotted with angular
velocity, all expressed in the same observer frame. Their sum is wrench power.
For two material points on the same rigid body, let $r_{AB}$ run from $A$ to $B$;
$F$ is the resultant force and $M_A,M_B$ its equivalent moments.
Then $v_B=v_A+\omega\times r_{AB}$ and $M_B=M_A-r_{AB}\times F$, so
$F\cdot v_B+M_B\cdot\omega=F\cdot v_A+M_A\cdot\omega$.
The separate force and moment powers can change even though the sum does not.
A change of observer is different: kinetic energy and power are frame dependent.
A point across a bending shaft need not satisfy this rigid-body velocity relation. Reporting only the couple may miss positive translational power;
reporting only net force may miss a large rotational exchange.

For two hands, individual contact powers can also be calculated. Their sum must
match net wrench power after consistent transformations and inclusion of any
contact moments, provided the contacts share the rigid-body motion used in the
reduction. With slip, local deformation or distinct hand/club velocities, retain
those contact powers and losses explicitly. That closure is a strong audit. Yet individual hand power does
not identify which muscle supplied it, because work can cross wrist, elbow,
shoulder, and trunk pathways and because co-contraction can add internal cost
without changing net external power.

### A Late Negative-Couple Example

Suppose the net force supplies +900 watts of translational club power while the
two-hand couple supplies -150 watts of rotational power over a short interval.
Net hand power remains +750 watts. The negative couple is real and locally
absorptive, but the hands as a whole still add club energy. If the couple changes
orientation so its power later becomes positive, its integrated work may be
near zero while its angular impulse is nonzero. A change in angular momentum
requires the sum of all external moments about a consistently chosen inertial
origin (or a separately justified center-of-mass balance).

Now run a matched-state branch without that couple. The club may release sooner,
changing geometry and reducing later positive power from another channel. The
baseline could then finish faster despite the early negative work. That result
would not mean negative work created energy; it would mean the intervention
changed the route and timing by which other work acted.

### Segment Work Is Not Muscle Work

Inverse dynamics produces net joint moments consistent with measured motion and
external loads under a model. For a rotational joint, dot the net moment acting
on the distal segment with its angular velocity **relative to the proximal
segment**, expressed in a common frame. This gives the joint’s net rotational
power; moments dotted with absolute segment velocities instead describe the
separate segment power flows. Include translational joint power if relative
translation is allowed. Several muscles, passive
tissues, contact loads, and model residuals can contribute to that moment.
Biarticular muscles can absorb energy at one joint and generate it at another.
Assigning net joint work to one named muscle is therefore not warranted.

Musculoskeletal optimization can propose allocations, and EMG can constrain
activation timing, but redundancy remains. A strong report keeps rigid-body
joint work, muscle-tendon work, and metabolic energy on separate evidence
levels. This distinction is especially important for claims about wrists
“resisting passively” or scapular muscles “creating” a club couple.

### Numerical Closure Before Storytelling

First declare the resolved mechanical energy: kinetic energy plus the chosen
gravitational and elastic potentials. A club-only boundary receives hand work;
a golfer-plus-club boundary instead contains actuators or muscles that convert
chemical energy into mechanical energy internally. “Closed” to mass does not
mean mechanically isolated or unable to perform internal work.

A useful smooth-phase ledger is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta E_{\rm mech}
&= W_{\rm boundary,nc}\\
&\quad+W_{\rm internal\ actuation}\\
&\quad-E_{\rm dissipated}.
\end{aligned}
$$

where “nc” denotes the nonconservative boundary channel, and
$E_{\rm dissipated}\geq0$ is mechanical energy converted into unresolved heat
or other dissipative modes. Boundary work excludes forces already represented by the included
potentials, and internal actuation excludes elastic storage already counted in
$E_{\rm mech}$. This equation assumes no unlisted mass flow, time-varying
potential or other energy conversion. Use a separate jump balance for impacts
rather than integrating across an unresolved impulse. For a passive full club
including its shaft, hand and aerodynamic work feed kinetic, gravitational and
shaft elastic energy plus dissipative losses. For the combined body and club,
hand-interface work cancels internally when contact motion is compatible, but
muscle/actuator conversion remains. Adding gravity work while also treating
gravitational potential $U_g$ as a destination would double-count it. Adding shaft storage to an energy
that already includes it would do the same.

Calculate closure over the whole trial and important phases. Report
absolute residual and residual relative to the effect being discussed. A 2 J residual may look small compared with total swing energy yet be fatal to a
claimed 1 J mechanism.

Timestep refinement, alternate differentiation/filtering, and independent
power calculations should preserve the conclusion. Agreement from two quantities
derived from the same filtered motion is an internal consistency check; it is
not an independent validation of the assumed mass properties or contact model. At contact interfaces,
action-reaction and power consistency provide additional checks. A model that
cannot close its ledger should not explain an unexpected sign by inventing a
new transfer narrative.

### What to Compare Across Strategies

For the arm-dominant and wrist-dominant extremes, compare more than terminal
speed. Plot bilateral forces and moments; common and differential hand modes;
interface power; cumulative work; club and body energy; shaft strain energy;
joint load proxies; and face/path sensitivity. Align comparisons by both clock
and state. Match the final club task when asking about internal allocation, and
match the initial state when asking about causal input contribution.

A role reversal may preserve net club work while changing peak force, internal
co-contraction, or timing sensitivity. Those are scientifically interesting
differences even if clubhead speed barely changes. Conversely, a small speed
gain may be unattractive if it depends on fragile timing or unmeasured internal
load.

### A Reviewer Can Recompute the Claim

The most useful release contains time, state, forces, moments, velocities,
powers, cumulative works, energy terms, and residuals in machine-readable form.
Units and frames live in a schema, and each figure links to its source. A reviewer
can then verify dot products and integrals instead of accepting a caption. This
is how a casual explanation remains connected to a scientific product.

### Reader Lab: Recompute a Power Ledger

Download one time series of force, moment, reference-point linear velocity, and
angular velocity. Check units and frames, then calculate translational power,
rotational power, and their sum sample by sample. Numerically integrate each with
at least two reasonable quadrature rules and compare. A difference larger than
the reported mechanism needs explanation.

Next transform the wrench and velocity to another point on the same rigid club
segment, keeping the observer fixed, and verify summed power is invariant. Reverse the declared swing-normal axis and confirm only the
coordinate label changes, not the physical power. Compare cumulative hand work
with the declared club energy and losses: count gravity and shaft storage once,
include any power crossing a cut through a flexible shaft, and retain the
residual with its sign.

Finally, shorten and lengthen the integration window. If a claimed positive
contribution depends entirely on an unreported boundary choice, the conclusion
must name that interval. This exercise is simple enough for a reviewer and
powerful enough to expose many sign and synchronization errors.

### The Difference Between Necessary and Sufficient

For a constant-mass particle in an inertial frame, increasing kinetic energy
requires positive net force work.
For an articulated system’s total mechanical energy, the required positive
balance may come from boundary work or internal chemical/actuator conversion,
after accounting for potentials and losses. Neither statement makes one
particular joint-power peak necessary: other routes can substitute. A negative couple may be sufficient to alter release in
one model but not necessary for all high-speed trajectories. Counterfactuals and
alternative allocations establish these logical distinctions.

Use cautious language: “contributed under this decomposition,” “improved the
declared outcome in this branch,” or “was associated in this sample.” Avoid
“caused all transfer” unless interventions and closure exclude competing paths.
The strength of the claim should match the design.

### A Compact Reporting Template

Name the system, boundary, reference point, frame, sign, and interval. Report
force and moment, point and angular velocity, power, cumulative work, energy
change, residual, and uncertainty. State whether each quantity is measured,
inferred, or simulated. Then link the machine-readable series. This template is
short enough for every mechanism result and prevents most category errors.

## Where the Picture Breaks

The suitcase treats the hand as one contact and the object as rigid. In golf,
two hands, a flexible shaft, and moving joint centers complicate the boundary.
Work at one reference must be transformed consistently, and distributed contact
may store energy locally.

Mechanical work also does not judge usefulness. Negative work can be essential
for control, accuracy, or preparing a favorable state. Positive work at the wrong
time can worsen the final task.
